lessons.title: Setting up your block moulds: wooden vs. metal moulds
lessons.body: Before you make blocks, you need a mould. You can buy one or make it yourself. The two main types are wooden and metal. Wooden moulds are cheaper and easier to make if you have basic carpentry skills. Use hardwood like mahogany or iroko, not softwood like pine, because softwood warps when wet. A standard wooden mould for a 6-inch block (15 cm x 20 cm x 40 cm) costs about $20Ã¢Â€Â“$30 in materials. But wooden moulds wear out fasterÃ¢Â€Â”after 200Ã¢Â€Â“300 blocks, the edges round off and blocks become uneven. Metal moulds, usually made from 2Ã¢Â€Â“3 mm steel sheet, cost $50Ã¢Â€Â“$100 but last for thousands of blocks. They keep their shape better, so your blocks are more uniform. If you plan to sell blocks, invest in metal. For a small backyard project, wood is fine. When setting up, make sure the mould is square: measure diagonalsÃ¢Â€Â”they must be equal. Bolt or screw all joints tightly. Any gap larger than 1 mm will let mortar leak and create weak edges. For mass production, build a mould that makes 2 or 3 blocks at once. A 3-block metal mould can cost $150 but triples your output. Set the mould on a flat, level surfaceÃ¢Â€Â”a wooden pallet or concrete slab. If the ground is uneven, blocks will be different thicknesses. Also, decide if you want a bottom plate or if you will cast on the ground. A bottom plate makes moving easier but adds cost. In Africa, many artisans use a simple wooden mould with a removable base. Whatever you choose, keep the mould clean and oiled (next lesson). Check for wear weekly. Replace or repair any bent sides. A good mould is the backbone of block making.

lessons.title: Preparing the mould: oiling and cleaning for easy release
lessons.body: If you skip oiling, your blocks will stick, and you will break corners trying to remove them. Oil creates a thin barrier so the concrete does not bond to the mould. Use any light oil: used engine oil, palm oil, or commercial release agent. Used engine oil is cheap and works well, but it stains the blocks dark. If you want clean-looking blocks, use vegetable oil or a proper mould oil. Apply oil with a rag or brush. Coat all inside surfaces, especially corners and edges. Do not pour oilÃ¢Â€Â”just a thin film. Too much oil can cause surface bubbles. Clean the mould after every use. Scrape off stuck concrete with a wooden scraper or wire brush. Do not use a metal hammerÃ¢Â€Â”it dents the mould. Rinse with water and dry. Then oil again before the next block. If you are making many blocks, oil the mould every 5Ã¢Â€Â“10 blocks, or whenever you see the mix starting to stick. In hot, dry weather, oil evaporates faster, so oil more often. For wooden moulds, oil also protects the wood from water damage. But do not soak the woodÃ¢Â€Â”too much oil can soften it. A good routine: after demoulding, clean the mould immediately while concrete is still green (soft). Then oil it and set it aside for the next batch. If you are using a manual machine, follow the manufacturer's instructionsÃ¢Â€Â”some machines need grease on moving parts, not oil on the mould faces. Keep a small bucket of oil and a rag near your work area. A dirty, rusty mould will ruin your blocks. In Africa, where dust and sand are common, cover your moulds when not in use to keep them clean. Proper preparation takes 2 minutes per mould but saves hours of frustration.

lessons.title: Filling and compacting the mix for solid blocks
lessons.body: Filling and compacting is where strength is made or lost. Your mix should be stiffÃ¢Â€Â”like damp sand that holds its shape when squeezed. A typical mix for solid blocks is 1 part cement to 6 parts sand (by volume) for a 6-inch block. For stronger blocks, use 1:5. Add water gradually; too much water weakens the block. A good test: squeeze a handfulÃ¢Â€Â”it should form a ball that does not crumble or drip water. Now fill the mould. Use a shovel or trowel to place the mix in layers. For a 6-inch block, fill halfway (about 10 cm deep), then compact. Compaction removes air pockets. Use a wooden tamper or a steel rod. Tamp evenly across the surfaceÃ¢Â€Â”about 20Ã¢Â€Â“25 strokes per layer. Do not just poke; lift the tamper and drop it. For the second layer, fill to the top of the mould and tamp again. Overfill slightly (1Ã¢Â€Â“2 cm) because the mix will settle. Then strike off the excess with a straight edge (a piece of wood or steel). Move the straight edge in a sawing motion across the top. Do not press down hardÃ¢Â€Â”just level it. For hollow blocks, you will use a core (a metal or wooden insert) to create voids. But for solid blocks, you want a dense, uniform fill. If you see voids or honeycomb after demoulding, you did not compact enough. In Africa, many makers use a manual vibration method: tap the sides of the mould with a hammer or lift the mould 2Ã¢Â€Â“3 cm and drop it on the ground 10 times. This settles the mix. But be carefulÃ¢Â€Â”too much dropping can cause segregation. After filling and compacting, let the block sit for 10Ã¢Â€Â“15 minutes before moving. This allows initial set. Then demould (next lesson). Remember: a well-compacted block is 30% stronger than a poorly compacted one. Take your time.

lessons.title: Using a manual block-making machine vs. hand tamping
lessons.body: You have two main options for compacting: a manual block-making machine or hand tamping. A manual machine (like a CINVA-Ram or a local copy) uses a lever to compress the mix. It costs $200Ã¢Â€Â“$500 but produces denser, stronger blocks and is faster. With a machine, you fill the mould, pull the lever, and the block is compressed with high pressure. You can make 200Ã¢Â€Â“400 blocks per day with a team. Hand tamping uses a wooden or metal tamper to compact the mix manually. It is cheap (a tamper costs $5) but slowerÃ¢Â€Â”maybe 50Ã¢Â€Â“100 blocks per day. Hand tamping also gives less consistent density; some blocks will be stronger than others. If you are building a house for yourself, hand tamping is fine. If you are selling blocks, a machine pays for itself in a few months. But machines need maintenance: grease the moving parts, check the lever, and replace worn parts. In rural Africa, where spare parts are hard to find, a simple wooden tamper is more reliable. You can also make a simple vibrating table from a small motor and a metal plate. That costs $100Ã¢Â€Â“$200 and works well for small production. The key difference is pressure. A manual machine applies 2Ã¢Â€Â“5 MPa (megapascals) of pressure; hand tamping gives maybe 0.5Ã¢Â€Â“1 MPa. Higher pressure means you can use less cement (1:7 mix instead of 1:6) and still get strong blocks. But for beginners, start with hand tamping to learn the feel of the mix. Then upgrade to a machine when you have consistent sales. Whichever you choose, the goal is a dense block with no voids. Test your blocks: drop one from waist height onto a hard surface. If it shatters, your compaction or mix is wrong. If it stays intact, you are doing well.

lessons.title: Removing blocks from moulds without breaking corners
lessons.body: Removing blocks too early or roughly is the number one cause of broken corners. Wait until the block is firm enough to hold its shape but still soft enough to release easily. This is usually 10Ã¢Â€Â“30 minutes after compaction, depending on weather. In hot, dry weather, it might be 10 minutes; in cool, humid weather, 30 minutes. Test by pressing the top of the block with your thumb. If it leaves a slight dent but does not crumble, it is ready. To remove, first loosen the mould. For a wooden mould, tap the sides gently with a rubber mallet or a block of wood. Do not use a metal hammerÃ¢Â€Â”it will crack the wood. For a metal mould, you may have a release mechanism (a lever or a screw). If not, tap the sides. Then lift the mould straight up. Do not twist or tiltÃ¢Â€Â”that breaks corners. If the block sticks, do not force it. Wait 5 more minutes and try again. If it still sticks, your oiling was insufficient. Next time, oil more. For a bottomless mould (casting on the ground), you lift the mould off the block. For a mould with a bottom plate, you flip the whole thing over onto a pallet or board, then lift the mould. Always lift the mould, not the block. After demoulding, leave the block on a flat pallet in the shade for 24 hours. Do not move it. Then cure it by watering it twice a day for 7 days. Broken corners mean wasted cement and time. A good demoulder can remove 200 blocks per day with less than 5% breakage. In Africa, many use a simple wooden mould with a removable base. Practice on a few blocks first. If you break one, remix itÃ¢Â€Â”do not throw it away. With practice, you will get a feel for the right time.

lessons.title: Making special blocks: hollow, solid, and interlocking types
lessons.body: Once you master solid blocks, you can make special types that save cement, reduce weight, or speed up construction. Hollow blocks have two or three vertical voids. They use 30Ã¢Â€Â“40% less cement and are lighter, so they are easier to carry. To make them, you need a mould with coresÃ¢Â€Â”metal or wooden inserts that create the holes. Fill the mould around the cores, compact, and remove the cores after demoulding. A standard hollow block (6-inch) has two voids, each about 10 cm x 15 cm. The wall thickness should be at least 3 cm for strength. Hollow blocks are popular in Africa because they save money. Interlocking blocks have a tongue-and-groove shape so they fit together without mortar. They are faster to build and stronger in earthquake zones. But they require a precise mould, usually metal, and a strong mix (1:5 cement to sand). You can buy interlocking moulds for $100Ã¢Â€Â“$300. They are common in East Africa (e.g., the "Interlocking Stabilised Soil Block" or ISSB). You can also make solid blocks with a decorative faceÃ¢Â€Â”just add a metal plate with a pattern to the mould. For all special blocks, the mix must be consistent. Use a measuring box (a 20-litre bucket) for cement and sand. Do not guess. Curing is critical: hollow and interlocking blocks need 14 days of curing because they have less mass. Water them twice a day. Test each batch: break one block after 7 days. If it breaks easily, increase cement. In Africa, many artisans make hollow blocks with a simple wooden core. Start with one type, perfect it, then expand. Remember: special blocks sell for 20Ã¢Â€Â“50% more than solid blocks, so they are worth learning.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Block Curing, Testing and Costing for African Markets

Curing is the step most small block yards in Africa get wrong, and it is the step that decides whether your blocks earn money or become rubble. A block that looks perfect on the pallet can lose 40â60% of its design strength if it dries too fast in the sun, is stacked too early, or is made with dirty water. This lesson gives you the numbers, the tests, and the costing model you need to run a block yard as a business â not a hobby.

The practical rule for a commercial yard: cure 7 days minimum, sell at 14 days, and never sell a block you have not broken in a test. Everything below supports that rule with field-ready figures.

Why curing is a business decision, not a technical detail

In most African markets â Nairobi, Kampala, Lusaka, Accra, Kigali â a 6-inch solid block sells for between USD 0.35 and USD 0.90 depending on cement content and finish. The cement is 55â75% of your variable cost. If your curing is bad, you do not lose the cement cost â you lose the whole block, and you lose the customer who bought it. A single failed wall in a school or church project can cost a yard its reputation for years.

Two numbers drive your margin: cement per block and breakage rate. A well-run yard keeps breakage under 3%. A poorly run yard runs 15â25% during demoulding and transport. That difference is the entire profit margin on a small yard.

Data table 1: Typical mix ratios and 28-day strength for common African block types

Block type Cement : sand : aggregate Cement per 6" block Target 28-day strength Typical use
Solid load-bearing 1 : 4 : 4 0.9â1.1 kg 3.5â5.0 N/mmÂ² Foundation, load walls
Solid non-load-bearing 1 : 6 : 6 0.6â0.7 kg 2.0â2.8 N/mmÂ² Partition walls
Hollow 6" 1 : 5 : 5 0.7â0.8 kg 2.5â3.5 N/mmÂ² General walls
Interlocking (dry-stack) 1 : 4 : 3 1.0â1.2 kg 4.0â6.0 N/mmÂ² Low-cost housing
Soil-cement (stabilised) 1 : 10 (cement : soil) 0.4â0.5 kg 1.5â2.5 N/mmÂ² Rural single-storey

Sources: Adapted from FAO/ILO small-scale blockmaking guidance, Practical Action technical briefs on building materials, and Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) block strength classes. Cement quantities assume 6-inch (150 mm) blocks; adjust for 4-inch and 8-inch sizes.

Data table 2: Cost and margin model for a small yard (per 1,000 blocks)

Cost item Quantity Unit cost (USD) Total (USD) Notes
Cement (OPC 42.5) 900 kg (18 bags) 7.00 / 50 kg bag 126.00 At 0.9 kg/block
Sand 4 tonnes 12.00 / tonne 48.00 Local river sand
Aggregate (6â10 mm) 3 tonnes 18.00 / tonne 54.00 Crushed stone
Water ~600 L 0.50 / 20 L 15.00 Clean, not saline
Labour (3 workers Ã 4 days) 12 person-days 4.00 / day 48.00 Mix, mould, cure
Mould / machine wear â â 10.00 Provision
Total cost â â 301.00 Per 1,000 blocks
Breakage allowance (5%) 50 blocks â â Only sell 950
Selling price 950 blocks 0.55 522.50 Typical East African price
Gross margin â â 221.50 ~42% margin

Sources: Cost structure adapted from FAO/ILO small-scale enterprise case studies and Practical Action market surveys for East African building materials. Prices are indicative and vary by country and season.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CEMENT AND DUST

Cement is strongly alkaline (pH ~12â13). Direct skin contact causes chemical burns, and wet cement inside boots or gloves is the most common cause of serious injury on small block yards. Dry cement dust irritates eyes and lungs and can cause silicosis with long-term exposure. Always wear waterproof gloves, boots, eye protection, and a dust mask when mixing. Never kneel in wet mortar. Wash any cement-contaminated skin immediately with clean water. Keep cement bags away from children and store them dry and off the ground. If cement enters the eye, rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help.

Field tests you can do without a lab

You cannot afford a compression testing machine on a small yard. But you can use three field tests that catch 90% of bad batches before they reach a customer:

1. The drop test. Take a cured block (14 days), lift it to chest height, and drop it flat onto a hard surface. A good load-bearing block cracks but does not shatter. If it breaks into three or more pieces, your mix is too lean or your curing was too fast.

2. The scratch test. Scratch the block face with a nail. If it powders easily, the cement has not hydrated properly â usually too little water during curing, or curing was skipped. If it resists and leaves a shallow mark, it is sound.

3. The water drop test. Drop a small amount of water on the block face. If it is absorbed in under 5 seconds, the block is porous and will need plastering. If it beads slightly and absorbs over 10â20 seconds, the surface is dense enough for exposed work.

Do these tests on 1 in every 500 blocks, or at least once per production day. Record the results in a notebook. When a customer complains, you have data â and data protects your reputation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Clean water only. No saline, no muddy, no recycled wash water on finished blocks.
  • Shade for the first 48 hours. Direct sun cracks blocks before they gain strength.
  • Water 2Ã daily for days 1â7, then 1Ã daily until day 14. Keep burlap or grass cover damp.
  • Do not stack higher than 4 blocks in the first week. Stack higher only after day 8.
  • Never sell before day 14. Sell at day 14â21 for best strength and lowest breakage.
  • Test 1 in 500 blocks with the drop, scratch, and water tests. Record results.
  • Keep 5% breakage allowance in your pricing. If breakage exceeds 10%, fix the mix or curing.
  • Wear gloves, boots, eye protection, and a dust mask every time you handle cement or mix dry materials.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale production of building materials (cement blocks and stabilised soil blocks)
  • Practical Action â Technical briefs on building materials and blockmaking
  • ILO â Small-scale enterprise development and construction sector guides
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â Masonry block standards and strength classes
  • WHO â Occupational health guidance on cement dust and construction site safety

Business takeaway: curing is free â it costs you time and shade, not money. The yard that cures properly sells every block it makes. The yard that rushes sells half its production as rubble. Build your curing shed before you buy your second mould.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a block mould that will be used for thousands of blocks?
quiz.explanation: Metal moulds last longer and keep their shape better than wood.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of oiling a block mould?
options: A) To make the block stronger
B) To prevent the concrete from sticking
quiz.explanation: Oil creates a barrier so the block releases easily without breaking.

quiz.q: How can you test if your concrete mix has the right amount of water?
options: A) It should be runny like soup
B) It should form a ball that holds shape when squeezed
C) It should crumble when squeezed
D) It should drip water when squeezed
quiz.explanation: A stiff mix that holds shape is ideal for strong blocks.

quiz.q: What is the typical cement-to-sand ratio for a solid 6-inch block?
quiz.explanation: A 1:6 mix is standard for solid blocks; 1:5 gives stronger blocks.

quiz.q: How many strokes of a tamper are recommended per layer when hand compacting?
quiz.explanation: About 20Ã¢Â€Â“25 strokes per layer removes air pockets effectively.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a manual block-making machine over hand tamping?
options: B) It produces denser, stronger blocks
D) It works faster in all conditions
quiz.explanation: Machines apply higher pressure, resulting in denser blocks.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before removing a block from the mould?
quiz.explanation: The block should be firm but still soft enough to release easily.

quiz.q: What tool should you use to tap a wooden mould to loosen it?
quiz.explanation: A rubber mallet loosens the mould without damaging the wood.

quiz.q: How much cement can hollow blocks save compared to solid blocks?
quiz.explanation: Hollow blocks use less material because of the voids.

quiz.q: What is a common interlocking block type in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: ISSB and Hydraform are both interlocking block systems used in Africa.

quiz.q: Why is curing important for hollow blocks?
quiz.explanation: Curing allows cement to hydrate and gain strength.

quiz.q: What is the minimum wall thickness for a hollow block?
quiz.explanation: At least 3 cm ensures adequate strength.

quiz.q: How often should you oil a mould when making many blocks?
quiz.explanation: Oiling every 5Ã¢Â€Â“10 blocks keeps release easy without excess oil.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your mix is too wet?
options: A) It holds shape when squeezed
B) It drips water when squeezed
quiz.explanation: Excess water weakens the block and causes dripping.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a core in a block mould?
quiz.explanation: Cores create voids, making hollow blocks.

quiz.q: How many blocks per day can a manual machine typically produce?
quiz.explanation: With a team, a manual machine can produce 200Ã¢Â€Â“400 blocks daily.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after demoulding a block?
options: A) Move it to direct sun
B) Leave it on a flat pallet in the shade
C) Stack it with other blocks
quiz.explanation: Blocks need to sit undisturbed in the shade for initial set.

quiz.q: What is a good test for block strength after 7 days?
quiz.explanation: A drop test shows if the block shatters or stays intact.

quiz.q: Which oil is cheap but stains blocks dark?
quiz.explanation: Used engine oil works but leaves dark stains.

quiz.q: What is the recommended curing period for solid blocks?
quiz.explanation: Solid blocks need 7 days of watering; hollow blocks need 14.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of interlocking blocks?
quiz.explanation: Interlocking blocks fit together without mortar, speeding construction.

quiz.q: How can you check if a mould is square?
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals confirm the mould is square.

quiz.q: What happens if you use too much oil on a mould?
quiz.explanation: Excess oil can cause bubbles on the block surface.

quiz.q: What is a simple vibrating table made from?
options: B) A small motor and metal plate
quiz.explanation: A small motor attached to a metal plate creates vibration.

quiz.q: Why should you not use a metal hammer on a wooden mould?
options: B) It dents and damages the wood
C) It makes too much noise
quiz.explanation: Metal hammers can crack or dent wooden moulds.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a simple wooden mould?
quiz.explanation: Wooden moulds are cheaper, costing about $20Ã¢Â€Â“$30 in materials.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a 1:5 mix instead of 1:6?
quiz.explanation: More cement makes the block stronger.

quiz.q: How should you store moulds when not in use?
quiz.explanation: Covering prevents dust and rust.

quiz.q: What is the first step after filling the mould with mix?
quiz.explanation: Compaction removes air pockets and densifies the mix.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good compaction?
quiz.explanation: A smooth, dense surface indicates proper compaction.
